blogs.name: Stratechery by Ben Thompson
blogs.title: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description:
Listen to this post: Good morning,

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi. Goodarzi took a…
blogs.content:
Listen to this post:

 Good morning,

 This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi . Goodarzi took a very non-traditional path to Silicon Valley, joining Intuit in 2004 after working at Siemens and Honeywell. After managing business units across the company he became CEO in 2019, and is taking on the challenge of figuring out how one of tech’s oldest software companies manages the AI paradigm shift.

 In this interview we discuss Goodarzi’s background and the what it takes to be an effective generalist, and get his take on how Intuit has thrived for 44 years. We discuss the shift from Quicken to Quickbooks, the TurboTax business, and how Goodarzi thinks about the consumer space today. Then we talk about accountants, Intuit’s most important customer acquisition channel, and how the company wants to change the profession from partners to customers via AI. I present the case to Goodarzi that Intuit seems like its being disrupted, and he makes the case why they are well positioned to actual grow their market. We also touch on acquisitions like Credit Karma and Mailchimp, and how Intuit has managed business model changes in the past, and what needs to change in the future.

 As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

 On to the Interview:

 An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI

 This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

 Topics:

 Being a Generalist | Intuit History | TurboTax and Credit Karma | The Future of Accountants | Disruption | Mailchimp | Intuit’s AI Future

 Being a Generalist

 Sasan Goodarzi, welcome to Stratechery.

 Sasan Goodarzi: Thank you for having me, I’m a big fan of all the work that you do. It’s great to be a part of it.

 Well, we’ll get to my relationship with Intuit, which I’ve had for many years. Big fan? I’m going to have to think about that one. We are here to talk about Intuit, a company that you have been at, with a brief break, for over 20 years. Before we get to that, however, tell me about your background, which is a very interesting one. Let’s start with where you were born.

 SG: Yes, I was born in Tehran, in Iran, and I am the youngest of three — 13 years younger than the other two brothers. I was told I was special, I think I was an accident, so there you go. And back then, you’d ship your kids to the U.S. because everybody wanted to come to the U.S. to study and so my brothers were in the U.S. already studying, and my parents decided to do an experiment with me and shipped me to the U.S. at the age of nine and I was very fortunate, because the revolution actually happened.

 Got it. So you had already left before then, I wasn’t quite sure on that timing.

 SG: Yeah, yeah. I was very fortunate, I left before the revolution, about eight to nine months before the revolution, and have been in the U.S. ever since.

 Where did you end up in the U.S.?

 SG: I came to Orlando, Florida of all places, because my brothers were going to the University of Central Florida. And, by the way, back then we used to say, “U Can’t Finish”, that’s what we called it, but it’s a great university. But anyways, for that reason, I was in Orlando until my early 20s, until I started being moved by Honeywell. Every couple of years, I was going to a different state, which was a lot of fun, and eventually ended up in California.

 You studied electrical engineering, right? And then you were at Honeywell and Invensys. What were you doing there? I mean, it doesn’t seem quite the obvious path to being CEO of Intuit, to say the least.

 SG: Not at all. In fact, it’s advice I give, career advice I give to folks. I actually started at Siemens, I was a technical marketing person, which really — I don’t know why they called it marketing, it was all a technical role that supported our field sales folks. I was in the power generation business unit at Siemens so I used to go pitch why our power generation was better than anybody else’s.

 I don’t think they need much marketing these days in the Siemens Power Generation Unit.

 SG: (laughing) Yeah that’s right, they don’t. I did that for four years and frankly, I didn’t know what I wanted to do with my life, because in the meantime, I was doing startups on the side. In fact, before I even started at Siemens, I did a startup called Lazer Cables — with, at that time, a very good friend that was actually the genius behind the idea of fiber optics for the music industry, so I was dabbling in a lot of different stuff.

 When I was at Siemens, I love the company, but I was wondering, “Is the corporate world cut out for me?”, and I got recruited to Honeywell. And at Honeywell, they put me — it was like business development. In essence, they put me in charge of something they were experimenting with, which was just down my alley, because it was, in essence, a startup as part of Honeywell and I fell in love with the company because of that. I was there, I think like eight years.

 So is this — was this going to different states? Was that because Honeywell, being a defense contractor, they just have to source from everywhere? Is that the connection?

 SG: Yeah, but I was in the industrial home automation division. So if you look at my background, I’ve been in power generation, I’ve been in home and buildings automation, I’ve been in industrial, which means I was selling software and hardware at the time to oil companies that need to manage all of their oil and gas in the fields. I’ve been in all of those different industries and then, to your point, I got a call from Honeywell, so my whole background is enterprise and oil and gas and all those different industries.

 So my forte was getting into something and diagnosing quickly what was going on and what should we do about it, my expertise wasn’t in any one industry. And then, when at the time Intuit called me, I didn’t even know what the company was.

 Right. It’s a very non-obvious connection, so what did they see? How did they find you?

 SG: I think the reason they found me is, at the time, the CEO had come from GE Capital, Steve Bennett . And I think at the time, they were looking for folks that knew how to run businesses, not — these are their words, not mine — not a typical Silicon Valley grown-up leader, and that’s what attracted them to me. And I was trying to figure out what Intuit was, because, one, I had never served consumers, businesses — it was always enterprise. But I really fell in love with, at that time, the culture of the company and the leaders of the company. And when I joined, I’ve been here sort of ever since — 20-some-odd years.

 Well, you did leave briefly to be CEO of energy company Nexant. What advantages do you think you gained from not having at all a traditional Silicon Valley CEO background? And also, on the flip side, what challenges has that presented?

 SG: The biggest learning I had, which had to come innate because I was in a new job almost every three years, is curiosity — is going in and really diagnosing, really trying to get to the root cause of if something is going well, “Why?”, if it’s not going well, “Why?”. How do you assess the industry, the talent, the priorities? And so I became, only because I had to, a master of how to be curious and diagnose.

 Does this require a very systemic sort of thinking about the problem? What makes a good generalist? Because you, I mean, clearly you’re a generalist. So what makes that effective?

 SG: It is, in fact, what you just said. One, you have to be a systems thinker. You have to ask a lot of questions end-to-end, because, one, it’s not from one particular craft, and you don’t know the industry that well and so you have to ask a lot of questions. You have to understand what the customer problems are. Structurally, are you advantaged or disadvantaged? What kind of talent do you have? It requires a systems thinker.

 But I think the second is you learn how to hire great, great people. Why? Because you don’t know anything about the industry. Once you know what you got to go do, you need great people that know how to go do it, I think those are the advantages.

 The disadvantages can be that you don’t innately — like when I went from power generation business unit to serving oil and gas, they don’t have too many things in common, and so the disadvantage is intuitively, right off the bat, you wouldn’t know what to do. I think that’s the disadvantage.

 I would tell you, from what I have learned, I would take those disadvantages any day over a leader that’s curious, that can diagnose really, really well. Because it naturally — one of the things I love about Amazon is the Day 1 mentality. Every day is Day 1, and Day 1 truly is when you’re curious, and you’re trying to understand what’s going on, and what kind of impact can you have. Well, when you don’t know an industry, it is truly Day 1. If you know an industry very, very well, you actually have to work hard to ensure that you’re diagnosing versus, “I have the answers to everything”.

 I think people would generally think oil and gas, energy, tech, totally different. Is there, though, a commonality in terms of where the investment takes place and the marginal cost of serving customers over time? Is that similar, or are there still really important differences there?

 SG: There are a lot of similarities I have learned over time in terms of just how do you run a business.

 So it’s just general management is the commonality?

 SG: And, by the way, I actually think it applies in this environment more than ever, frankly, because structural advantages — are there any in this environment? What is your structural advantage? Making sure that you’re curious about how you really reinvent experiences because of what’s possible with AI.

 I think there’s a lot of commonalities, inclusive of — this is probably the biggest thing I would say when I came, and I have a lot of respect, by the way, for all the companies and all the leaders in the Valley because, frankly, we are the ecosystem that drives global innovation, period, end of story. With that said, I think one of the things I’ve learned over my career is we can end up being sloppy in the Valley in terms of how we think about expenses, how we think about cost, how we think about allocation of capital. Those are things you just — when you come from oil, gas, power generation, where margins are thin, room for error is zero because, trust me, you do one thing wrong in oil and gas, you can blow up oil tanks.

 And so those things carry forward in terms of how do you build quality software, where do you put your money. But then there are things that don’t carry over, which is oil and gas has nothing to do with how consumers consume stuff.

 Right. Can generalists — could it be a sort of weakness of generalists — you said sloppy. And I think about the generalist angle and systems thinking and it’s easy to skim over the details, “Not that important”. Is that a challenge that you sometimes think about?

 SG: First of all, I think every leader, no matter what industry, has to have helicopter skills. I think you have to — one, I don’t think you can set clear vision of where you need to go and then move fast to get there if you’re not grounded in details. What does that mean? I mean, for me, details are, are you meeting with customers? Are you in your KPIs? Are you using products? Are you looking around corners in terms of what has to happen in your experiences? I think you have to be detail-oriented, and not just in this environment, I think every senior leader at every level has to have detailed orientation.

 Systems thinking doesn’t mean you lack detail orientation, it just means that you’re thinking about a problem end-to-end and because one of the biggest things I learned at Honeywell is — think about building a plane, just as an illustr...

blogs.author: Zach Mink

blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,718 new readers. Got a phone call you’ve been putting off? Your AI agent might be ready to handle it for you, from the long hold times to the awkward small talk with whoever picks up.
 SpaceXSI’s Grok Bot just got the ability to hop on the phone for its paid users, and with rival agents moving in the same direction, sitting on hold (for humans) might soon be a thing of the past.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 SpaceXSI’s Grok Bot starts making phone calls

 Nate’s Notebook: Make AI sketch before it builds

 Which free AI tool should you actually use?

 Midterm voters turn on data centers, AI

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 SPACEXSI
 📞  SpaceXSI’s Grok Bot starts making phone calls
 Image source: SpaceXSI

 The Rundown: SpaceXSI just rolled out phone calls in Grok Bot, the company’s AI agent platform, which can now sit on hold, book appointments, and negotiate bills on U.S. numbers — with users legally responsible for every call the bot makes.
 The details:
 If a rep asks something the bot can’t answer, users get a message mid-call and type a reply for it to pass along, all while following a live transcript.

 SpaceXSI’s terms make users the “caller of record,” “solely responsible” for calls and for following phone laws, with bots disclosing they’re a “virtual assistant.”

 The calls appear to run directly inside the platform via a temporary number, with early examples including a Comcast bill negotiation and a pizza order .

 Grok Bot is available for paid users, and Elon Musk answered complaints about usage limits by calling the platform’s cost “unsustainably high relative to revenue.”

 Why it matters: AI labs keep pitching agents as a way to take annoying life tasks off people’s plates, and for many, phone calls sit near the top of that list. With Grok Voice already answering 20,000 Starlink calls a day by SpaceXSI’s own count, the phone could soon go the way of the agentic internet — bots talking with other bots.

 TOGETHER WITH BOX
 💡  BoxWorks: The next generation of enterprise AI

 The Rundown: Box is the single platform that securely connects your people, agents, and applications to your enterprise content. Today at BoxWorks 2026, they’ll unveil innovations to harness frontier AI and reimagine business processes, with content and security at their core.
 You’ll hear about:
 Box and NVIDIA powering enterprise intelligence

 Next-gen workflow automation and advanced threat detection

 Tailored AI solutions modernizing media & entertainment, banking, and public sector work

 Tune into BoxWorks today at 9 AM PT for live updates.

 NATE’S NOTEBOOK
 🗺️ Nate’s Notebook: Make AI sketch before it builds

 The Rundown:   Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.
 Nate: TED grew on two ideas. Make the world’s best and brightest distill their biggest idea into 18 minutes or less. Then help them with the visuals, because communicating complicated ideas with strong visuals takes a separate level of genius altogether. Nancy Duarte’s design team helped speakers rework their slides.
 If you’re on a $20 AI plan, you’ve probably had a few aha moments and started running out of credits. You also have an entire graphic design department sitting in that chat. Claude’s custom visuals and ChatGPT’s new Intelligent UI can drop a chart, table, or flow diagram right into the reply.
 Every session is finite, expiring intelligence. The question is where to thrash. Most people thrash way too late, trying to make huge swinging changes to a deck or website that’s already built. They burn their tokens, run out of credits, and still end up frustrated. You can’t change where the Mississippi River exits in Louisiana; you’ve got to change the trickle up top.
 So before anything gets built, I tell it: don’t start yet. This is where we’re eventually going, but conserve your energy until we agree on the path. Never give me more than a paragraph or two. Ask me smart multiple-choice questions, or better yet, sketch it right in the chat, so you can cut big chunks of work you’ll never have to do.

 AI TRAINING
 🆓  Which free AI tool should you actually use?

 The Rundown: ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and Perplexity all have free plans. But they offer different tools and limits. In this guide, you’ll run the same tasks in each one, check the results, and build a small AI toolkit without paying for the six.
 Step-by-step:
 Open the six services and check that each account is on its free plan. Use personal accounts and keep private work out of the test

 Paste the same fictional Repair Café brief into each assistant (all resources in the full guide ). Check the event time, staffing, budget, and missing details

 Ask each tool the same question about Shenandoah National Park. Open the official National Park Service source and check the leash rule and trail restrictions

 Upload the same small budget CSV wherever the free tier allows it. If uploads are unavailable, paste the data and record that limit separately

 Score each result for accuracy, source quality, file handling, and usefulness. Choose a main assistant, a research tool, and a backup based on results

 Pro tip: A free plan can be generous for chat but tight on uploads, image creation, or research. Check the limit that applies to the task you actually do.

 PRESENTED BY GOOGLE FOR STARTUPS
 🤖  Build scalable autonomous AI agents

 The Rundown: The new Startup guide to AI agents is a technical, code-first blueprint designed to help developers build, evaluate, and deploy robust multi-agent systems on Google Cloud using the Agent Development Kit (ADK).
 Inside the guide, you’ll discover how to:
 Shift from prompt to context engineering

 Optimize token costs across model tiers

 Implement rigorous AgentOps for production reliability

 Download the AI agents guide .

 AI & THE MIDTERMS
 ⛔️ Midterm voters turn on data centers, AI
 Image source: datacentersontheballot.com

 The Rundown: Voters in U.S. midterms backed limits on data centers almost everywhere those measures appeared on local ballots and handed Congress to Democrats, promising tougher oversight of Silicon Valley, with a majority also telling NBC they expect AI to do more harm than good.
 The details:
 Data center opponents have taken 38 of 39 fully counted local measures, according to election trackers, with only Harwood, N.D., voting the other way.

 In NBC’s exit poll , 76% of voters would oppose a data center going up in their own community, and 57% expect AI to hurt society more than help.

 Goldman Sachs reportedly sees 45% of planned U.S. data center capacity at risk of temporary freezes, but figures the political heat will cool over time.

 Elon Musk, the biggest midterm donor at $446M backing Republicans, posted that data centers in space look “pretty appealing right now,” following the results.

 Why it matters: The public has heavily rebuked AI and the data center buildout in the midterms. With AI infrastructure hubs like Texas flipping blue and Democrats about to run the hearings on AI regulation, the ground under the entire industry just shifted — and the days of a hands-off federal approach to U.S. AI labs are likely coming to an end.

blogs.description: Apple's earnings suggest that the company's hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?
blogs.content:
Apple's earnings suggest that the company's hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

Over on Asianometry , Jon explains The Rise of GLM and China’s Zhipu AI , and also gives a trip report from Silicon Valley .

On to the Update:

Apple Earnings

From the Wall Street Journal :

The Apple growth and profit machine is wavering, and the boost from price increases might not be enough to keep it going at historic rates. That dials up the pressure on Apple’s new chief executive, John Ternus. The company saved the bad news for its earnings call, an hour after it posted its results for the September quarter, projecting that for the current quarter its high-margin services business will continue to slow and that its widely watched gross profit margin will continue to fall.

Apple shares had been flat in post-close trading but declined as much as 4% after the company made the projections, which fell short of Wall Street estimates. The impact of high memory costs are weighing even more heavily on the company, Ternus and Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said on the company’s earnings call. Apple has stockpiled cheaper components purchased earlier, but those inventories are dwindling…

Investors have bid up Apple shares because it has been a port in the AI storm—a reliable and capital-efficient business that stands apart from rivals which are spending hundreds of billions of dollars racing to the AI frontier. While others invest in data centers, Apple has been pouring its own cash into buybacks and dividends. But that safety may be challenged if Ternus can’t speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

Actually, I thought that on his maiden earnings call Ternus made a good case that Apple’s innovation engine is running pretty well:

This is an amazing time at Apple. We just completed one of the most prolific launch periods in our history. It’s been a remarkable time for innovation across all of our categories. One of the greatest testaments to that is the all-new iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original. We’re also incredibly excited about iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which take massive leaps forward on camera, battery life, and performance—features that our users care deeply about. Meanwhile, touch has arrived on Mac for the first time with the all-new MacBook Pro. And we were excited to announce the new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. The all-new iPad mini features a stunning new OLED display and brings a super thin design to the smallest member of the iPad family. Apple Watch now offers users the clearest window yet into their heart health. We introduced AirPods 5, which feature industry-leading active noise cancellation in an open-ear design. And we’ve laid the foundation for an even more intelligent smart home with the all-new HomeView, Apple TV 4K, and HomePod mini.

That’s a lot of new products, and the headliner — the iPhone Duo — appears to be a big hit, murmurs about hinge issues notwithstanding. Speaking anecdotally, the response to the device amongst normal users is extremely positive, even if it doesn’t appeal to more hardcore users ; to the extent that is true, that’s a positive sign, in two regards: first, it’s a pleasant reminder that people who obsess over this stuff don’t always represent normal users, and second, there is still room for Apple to segment the market, not just by price but also through fundamental design (as for me, I’m waiting for the Air 2).

Meanwhile, the new MacBook Pro with touch is exactly the computer I’ve been hoping for ever since I first used computers with touch displays at Microsoft 15 years ago. What Microsoft got wrong with Windows 8 was that they overhauled the interface to be touch-first; yes, you can use a mouse-and-keyboard with a touch interface easily enough, but it’s too easy: you give up a lot of power and control in exchange for denominating the user interface by the least precise input method.

Apple didn’t do that: touch is just an extra interaction layer that is there when you need it, and not catered to when you don’t; that’s exactly where Microsoft ended up too, which is why nearly all high-end Windows devices still have touch, even if the operating system long ago reverted towards being built around precise mouse-and-keyboard interfaces. This isn’t a touch-screen computer; it’s a computer that you can touch when and if you find it convenient (and having used them, it’s very nice to have!).

---

Presented by

I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. Luckily, our new advertising partner Stripe has the unique position of processing the equivalent of 1.7% of global GDP, making it, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

Their latest SaaS data , for example, shows that while SaaS stocks were supposedly experiencing an apocalypse, revenue growth was actually accelerating. You can read about that disconnect on their Stripe Economics blog on Substack.

I suspect there’s a lot more hiding in Stripe’s data and I’m looking forward to having an excuse to dig into it.

---

Memory Problems

Apple first started pushing the narrative that they were a services company in 2016, but, as I argued at the time , that was more aspirational and narrative selling than reality, given the fact the stock market was still focused on iPhone sales; three years later, however, when Apple stopped reporting unit sales and started talking about its installed base I called the switch: Apple was a services company . Three years after that, I was shocked when the company didn’t raise prices in the face of inflation , but I shouldn’t have been: effectively lowering prices — which helps gain market share — is exactly the right approach to take if growing services is the top priority. Indeed, Apple continued to not (or barely) raise prices for years after that, and then came the memory crisis.

It was memory that dominated the Q&A on the earnings call, and it’s hitting Apple on multiple fronts. First, even with June’s price increases (which didn’t include the iPhone), margins were down by about one percentage point because of memory. Second, even with price increases both in September (on the iPhone) and October (on Macs and iPads, above and beyond the summer’s increase), margins will decrease by another 1.5–2 percentage points. Moreover, Ternus said it’s going to get worse:

Let me give you an overall view on memory. What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented, and as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now, for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So, as we said, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June, and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset. We also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well, as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we said before, we do believe we will see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. And there is one more thing I wanted to add. As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow. Now back to Kevan for the other parts of it.

That last bit is point number three: Apple is having to make significant purchase obligations to secure memory, likely locking in these high prices. Fourth, despite those purchase obligations — or perhaps because purchase obligations are necessary — Apple actually doesn’t have enough memory! This was COO Sabih Khan, the second new addition to the earnings call:

So during the September quarter, we experienced supply constraints on iPhone, Mac and iPad, and this was driven by the high levels of demand, and as we’ve said before, we’re seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal. The Q4 constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the advanced nodes our SOCs are produced on, but as we have transitioned more of our lineup to the latest 2nm technology nodes, our constraints on advanced nodes are easing. And for the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected.

I made this point previously in the context of those SoC constraints, which is that Apple isn’t just used to dictating price to suppliers, but also having the freedom to ramp its manufacturing up and down in response to demand while forcing those suppliers to maintain the capacity and inventory to meet their needs. Now, however, Apple has to actually forecast demand, knowing that if they forecast too low they won’t sell as much as they could have, and if they forecast too high they are the ones who have to carry excess inventory.

The Hardware Company Regression

The good news for Apple goes back to the innovation question: the company is consistently missing its forecasts by underestimating demand. Of course it would be ideal if the company had enough devices to sell to everyone who wanted one, as soon as they want it, but in the grand scheme of things it’s good news that Apple devices seem to be more popular than ever. Moreover, that popularity is increasing even as the price increases. CFO Kevan Parekh was, understandably, unwilling to say this was a trend:

If I kind of unpack the comments around supply chain, about availability of components, and your outlook for the December quarter, can you help us understand sort of the difference or maybe the delta of quantity versus price across the product lineup? Because it certainly looks like you’re looking at double digit growth across the iPhone and the Mac business, and we all know, I think, in the industry that there’s been pretty strong price inflation across the PC/Mac ecosystem, and you guys mentioned that you’ve reluctantly taken price as well. So can you help us understand kind of what’s the driving dynamics in that market?

KP : We don’t normally provide that level of detail or color as we look at the outlook, other than to say, again, we did guide to the 7% to 10% year on year, and again, just as a reminder, that is on top of a phenomenal December quarter last year, where revenue grew 16%, and so we don’t provide the level of detail, but I would say it’s early to really read price elasticity at this point in time. The iPad and Mac were constrained since we had made those adjustments, and again, we just recently just adjusted the price on iPhone, so it’s really early to really assess any elasticity impact at this stage.

This explains why I was so shocked when Apple didn’t raise prices four years ago; from the very beginning of Stratechery I’ve been wondering just how high Apple could raise prices without significantly hurting demand, and well, the seeming answer — just as it was with the iPhone 5S vs 5C, and just as it was with the iPhone X — is significantly higher!

There is, however, one fly in the ointment; this was the paragraph that came after Ternus’ opening extolling Apple’s hardware launches:

On top of it all, we’re unlocking more powerful AI experiences across our lineup, including with the all-new Siri AI, a profoundly capable and deeply personal assistant seamlessly integrated across our platforms. And like everything we make, Siri AI is built with essential privacy protections so no one can access users’ data, not even Apple. We launched Siri AI in beta for US English users in Septem...
